summary: This unit teaches you to plan, run and follow up meetings: to decide whether a meeting is needed and set its purpose, to plan who attends, the venue or platform and the notice, to build a timed agenda, to chair formal, online and hybrid meetings, to apply quorum, voting and conflict rules, to write minutes and an action log, and to check that decisions were carried out.

blocks.p: Meetings are one of the most expensive tools a manager uses, because every minute costs the pay of everyone in the room. This unit teaches you to decide whether a meeting is needed, to plan it, to chair it, to record it, and to make sure the decisions are carried out. It applies to staff meetings, committees, boards, project meetings and online meetings in businesses, schools, hotels and public bodies in Jamaica.
The unit is for supervisors and managers who call, chair or write up meetings. You will often do all three roles at different times, so you need to understand each one.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it means in practice
rows: Decide whether a meeting is needed
Set a clear purpose and outcome, and choose the right type of meeting or another way to communicate
Plan the meeting
Choose who attends, the date, time and venue (or platform), send notice, and prepare papers
Prepare the agenda
Order and time the items so that decisions get enough time, and send the agenda in good time
Include everyone
Make sure access, equipment and language needs are met, including for online and hybrid meetings
Chair the meeting
Keep to the agenda, time and rules; bring everyone in; handle conflict; help the meeting reach decisions
Follow meeting rules
Apply notice, quorum, motions, voting, declarations of interest and confidentiality correctly
Record the meeting
Write clear minutes and an action log, get them approved and keep them safely
Follow up and evaluate
Chase actions, measure whether the meeting worked and improve the next one

blocks.note: Meetings are governed by the organisation's own rules (standing orders, a constitution, articles or terms of reference) and by the law that applies to it. Always check your organisation's rules before you plan. This kit teaches the common good practice; where your rules differ, your rules and your instructor come first.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A meeting is the right tool when people need to **discuss, decide, solve a problem together, build agreement or share news that needs questions**. It is the wrong tool when the aim is only to pass on information that nobody will question. A short memo, email, notice board or message does that at a fraction of the cost.

head: Situation
Better choice
rows: Telling staff that a form has changed
Memo or email with the form attached
Getting a quick yes or no from one person
A call or message
Reaching a decision that affects the whole team
A meeting, with papers sent in advance
Solving a problem that needs several skills
A problem-solving meeting or a workshop
A confidential matter about one person
A private one-to-one meeting, not a group

blocks.p: Before anything else, write the **purpose** (why we are meeting) and the **outcome** (what must be true at the end). For example: purpose, to deal with late deliveries; outcome, an agreed plan with three actions, each with an owner and a date. If you cannot write the outcome in one sentence, you are not ready to call the meeting.

head: Type
Purpose
Features
rows: Briefing or team meeting
Share information, give instructions, take questions
Led by the manager; usually short; regular
Decision-making meeting
Reach a decision
Papers in advance; options and recommendation; a clear vote or consensus
Problem-solving meeting
Find causes and solutions
People who know the facts; facts shared first; actions at the end
Brainstorming session
Produce many ideas
Judging the ideas is kept for later; every idea is recorded
Project or progress meeting
Check progress against plan
Reports, risks, next steps; an action log
Committee or board meeting
Govern or oversee
Formal rules, quorum, motions, minutes
Annual general meeting (AGM)
Report to members and elect officers
Notice period set by the constitution or law; formal minutes
Review or evaluation meeting
Learn from what happened
Evidence; no blame; lessons recorded
Stand-up (huddle)
Quick daily alignment
5 to 15 minutes; often standing; no long debate
Online or hybrid meeting
Meet when people are in different places
Needs a platform, tested equipment and extra care from the chair

blocks.p: A **virtual meeting** is one in which every member joins from a different place through an online platform. A **hybrid meeting** mixes people in a room with people online. Choose the format by purpose, cost and who must take part.

head: Format
Best when
Watch out for
rows: Face-to-face
Sensitive or complex items, building a new team, workshops, items that need a lot of discussion or body language
Travel time and cost; people in other parishes may find it hard to attend
Online (virtual)
Short, focused items; people spread across Kingston, May Pen, Montego Bay and elsewhere; regular updates
Poor internet, distraction, harder to read the room; some people join less easily
Hybrid
Some members are near and some far, and the meeting needs both
Online members getting left out; needs good room equipment and a skilled chair

blocks.p: For a quarterly review of 12 supervisors from Kingston, May Pen and Montego Bay, a manager might hold one face-to-face meeting a year and online meetings for the other quarters, or hold a hybrid meeting with a host for the online group.

blocks.h: When to cancel or replace a regular meeting

blocks.p: A manager should **cancel or replace a regular meeting** when it has no real purpose, when nothing has changed since the last one, when the key people cannot attend, or when a cheaper way will do. Possible replacements: a short written update; a message group; a call with the one or two people concerned; or a short stand-up. Keep a meeting when a decision, discussion or problem-solving is really needed. Review regular meetings every few months and ask whether each one still earns its cost.

**Formal meetings** follow written rules: notice, agenda, quorum, motions, voting and minutes. Boards, committees, school boards, credit unions and AGMs are formal. **Informal meetings** (a team huddle, a quick check-in) have few rules but still need a purpose and a record of any actions. A manager must know which kind she is running, because the formal kind can be challenged if the rules are not followed.

head: Role
Main duties
rows: Chairperson
Leads the meeting; keeps to the agenda, time and rules; makes sure everyone can speak; sums up decisions
Secretary (or meeting secretary)
Prepares the notice and agenda with the chair, sends papers, keeps the attendance record, takes and drafts minutes, keeps the records
Members or participants
Read the papers, come prepared, contribute, follow the rules, carry out their actions
Presenter or item owner
Introduces an item with a short summary and a clear recommendation
Timekeeper (when used)
Tells the chair when an item's time is nearly used
Observer or guest
Attends for information; speaks and votes only if the rules allow

blocks.p: Good planning is what makes a meeting short and useful. Work through the steps below in order.

flow: Set the purpose and the outcome
Decide who needs to attend and for which items
Check the rules: notice, quorum, who may call the meeting
Choose date, time and venue or platform
Prepare the agenda and the papers
Send notice, agenda and papers on time
Confirm attendance and arrange access and equipment

blocks.p: Invite **the people who hold the facts, the authority to decide, or the task to be carried out**. Inviting everyone 'so nobody feels left out' wastes time and makes discussion slow. People who are needed only for one item can be invited for that item only. Others who must be told the result can read the minutes.

blocks.note: A member of staff costs the organisation money every hour. Counting the cost makes people take meetings seriously.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Choose a time when the key people are free and not rushed; avoid the busiest hour of the business day.
Allow enough time for the agenda, and no more. A meeting fills the time it is given.
Book the venue early. Check seating, ventilation, noise, lighting, power points, projector or screen, and refreshments if needed.
For a service business such as a shop or a clinic, arrange cover so that customers or patients are still served while staff are in the meeting.

blocks.p: Everyone entitled to attend must be able to take part. Plan for this at the start, not when someone arrives.

head: Need
What to arrange
rows: A member who uses a wheelchair or has limited mobility
Step-free entry, a ramp or lift, an accessible washroom, a seating place with space; check these before booking
Deaf or hard-of-hearing members
A sign language interpreter if requested, written papers, a loop or captions online, a seat where faces can be seen
Blind or low-vision members
Papers in large print or by email in a form a screen reader can use; someone to guide at the venue
Members who read slowly or have limited literacy
Short, plain papers; talk through important items
Members with caring or travel difficulties
Reasonable timing; online attendance if suitable

blocks.p: Ask in the notice: 'Please tell the secretary by [date] if you need any support to attend.'

The notice tells members the date, time, place (or link) and purpose, and normally comes with the agenda. **The organisation's rules say how much notice is needed** (for example five working days for a committee or a longer period for an AGM). If notice is too short, decisions made may be open to challenge. The planner should move the date, or follow the rule that allows short notice (for example all members agreeing in writing to waive it).

Papers support the items: reports, figures, quotations, a draft policy. Send them **with the notice and agenda, early enough for members to read them**. For a decision item, the paper should be short and should give the background, the options, the cost and a clear recommendation. A member who sees a J$2 million quotation for the first time at the table cannot make a sound decision.
Staff-time cost = number of people × cost per person per hour × hours.

head: Example
Working
Cost
rows: 6 supervisors, J$3,000 an hour each, 1 hour 30 minutes
The same meeting held every week for 48 weeks
Same meeting with only 4 people needed in the room

blocks.p: Staff time can also be counted in **person-hours**: people × hours. Eight people at a meeting of 1.5 hours use 8 × 1.5 = 12 person-hours. Multiply by the average hourly cost to get money.
The cost does not include rent, light, refreshments or lost sales. Use the figure to ask: is the result worth this much?

The agenda is the plan of the meeting. It tells members what will be discussed, in what order and, when it is timed, for how long. Sending it before the meeting lets members prepare. A meeting without an agenda drifts.

head: Item
What happens
rows: 1. Welcome and apologies
The chair opens; the secretary reports who has sent apologies for absence
2. Declarations of interest
Members say if they have a personal or financial interest in an item
3. Minutes of the last meeting
Members check them for accuracy and approve them, with any correction recorded
4. Matters arising
Follow-up on points in the last minutes and progress on earlier actions
5. Main items (decisions first)
The key reports and decisions, in order of importance
6. Reports for noting
Short items for information
7. Any other business (AOB)
Small points notified to the chair beforehand; not for major new decisions
8. Date of next meeting; close
The chair sums up and confirms the next date

ol: List every item, with the person who will introduce it.
Put **decision items early**, when people are fresh, and give them the most time.
Put routine and information items later, or in the papers as 'for noting'.
Add a time to each item and check that the total fits the meeting length.
Show for each item whether it is for decision, discussion or information.
Agree the draft with the chair before sending it.

blocks.p: To find when a timed meeting should end, add the item times and add them to the start time. A meeting starting at 9:30 a.m. with items of 10, 20, 30 and 15 minutes takes 75 minutes and should end at 10:45 a.m. Add time for any break.

Example, a one-hour management meeting: apologies and interests (3 minutes); minutes and matters arising (7); decision on the new duty roster (25); report on stock losses, for discussion (15); reports for noting (5); AOB and close (5). Total 60.

blocks.note: If the agenda has more items than the time allows, remove or move items before the meeting. Do not hope the chair will rush.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Matters arising** covers follow-up on the last minutes, such as whether an action was done. It is not a place to reopen a decision already made. **Any other business** is for minor points. A major new issue should go on a later agenda with proper papers.
A member who cannot attend should tell the secretary before the meeting. The secretary records the name as an apology. This also helps the chair check whether there will be a quorum.
Online meetings let people join from Kingston, Montego Bay, Negril or abroad without travel. They also bring technical and behaviour problems that the organiser must manage.

ul: Choose a platform that every member can use, and send the link and any password in the invitation.
Test the platform, microphone, camera and screen-sharing beforehand. Ask members to test theirs.
Send the agenda and papers early, as for any meeting.
Appoint a host or technical lead who admits people, mutes noise and helps those in trouble.
Agree a **deputy chair** to carry on if the chair's connection fails.
Agree a back-up: a telephone dial-in number, or a message group, if the internet fails.
Keep the link private. Use a waiting room or password so that only invited people join.
Ask members to mute when not speaking and keep cameras on when they can.
The chair calls speakers by name, uses a 'raise hand' feature and watches the chat.
Share the screen so that everyone sees the same paper or figures.
Pause often to ask if anyone has a question, because people online find it harder to interrupt.

blocks.p: In a **hybrid meeting** some people are in the room and some join online. The common problem is that **online members are left out**, because they cannot hear side comments or see faces. The chair should:

ul: use a room microphone and speaker that pick up everyone in the room, and a camera that shows the room;
ask people in the room to speak one at a time and not to hold side conversations;
invite online members to speak first or regularly, and check with them before closing each item;
share documents electronically, not only on paper.

blocks.note: Do not record a meeting without telling members and getting their agreement first. Say how the recording will be stored and who may see it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Many Jamaican workplaces have uneven internet signal, especially at remote sites. Always send a written update in advance from anyone likely to drop out, and keep a phone dial-in as a back-up.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The chair's main role is to **keep the meeting to its agenda, time and rules**, and to help it reach decisions. The chair is a facilitator, not the person who talks the most. In a committee the chair is expected to be fair to all views, even if she holds a strong opinion.

ul: Read the papers and know the likely issues.
Agree the agenda, papers and difficult points with the secretary beforehand.
Know the rules: quorum, how decisions are made, what the chair may do.
Think of what could go wrong: a dominating member, a heated item, missing papers.
Plan how long each item should take and where you will cut discussion.

flow: Check there is a quorum, then open the meeting
Take apologies and declarations of interest
Take items in agenda order; state the purpose of each
Invite the presenter, then discussion, then summarise
Seek a decision; confirm it and the action
Watch the time; defer items if needed
Sum up decisions and actions; confirm the next date; close

blocks.p: If halfway through it is clear that the agenda will run 30 minutes over, the chair should tell members and **agree with them which items to defer or shorten**, rather than rush the decisions.

A **quorum** is the smallest number of members who must be present for the meeting to make valid decisions. It is set in the rules. For example, if a committee's rules require six members and only four arrive, there is no quorum: the meeting may talk, but cannot make binding decisions. If quorum is lost during the meeting (a member leaves), decisions cannot be taken until it is restored.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Standing orders
The written rules for how the meeting is run
Motion
A proposal put to the meeting, usually in the form 'That ...'
Proposer and seconder
The person who puts the motion and a second person who supports it so that it can be debated
Amendment
A change to the wording of a motion; voted on before the main motion
Point of order
A member's claim that the rules are not being followed
Abstain
To choose not to vote
Casting vote
An extra vote some rules give the chair to break a tie
Adjourn
To stop the meeting and continue at another time
Resolution
A motion that has been passed

head: Problem
What the chair does
rows: One person talks over others on every item
Thank the member, then invite others to speak in turn; use a speaking order or time limit
A quiet member who has not spoken
Ask a direct, open question about her item or her experience
A long speaker repeats the same point
Summarise the point and move on: 'Thank you, that is noted. Who has a different view?'
Side conversations
Ask for one speaker at a time, or ask them to share the point with everyone
Phones and laptops distract
Agree rules at the start; take short breaks
A member becomes hostile or abusive

Stay calm, remind everyone of the ground rules, ask the member to address the issue not the person, call a short break if needed, then speak privately; if it continues, ask the member to leave or report it under the organisation's policy

head: Method
How it works
Best used when
rows: Consensus
Discussion until everyone can accept the decision
Everyone must live with the outcome, such as a duty roster; time allows
Majority vote
More than half vote for
A clear yes or no is needed and the rules allow it
Chair or manager decides after consultation
The manager listens, then decides
Speed matters; manager holds accountability
Delegation
A small group decides
The details need study

head: Decision
Suggested method
Reason
rows: A new staff welfare policy
Consultation and consensus, or a vote after discussion
People must live with it; time is available; support matters
An urgent safety problem
The manager or chair decides after quick advice from the people who know
Speed and accountability matter; consult only those needed

blocks.p: A decision should be **confirmed aloud and written down**: what was decided, who will act, by when. If a vote is tied, what happens next depends on **the meeting's rules or standing orders** (for example a casting vote for the chair, or the motion fails).

Disagreement about ideas helps a meeting. Disagreement that becomes personal does not. If two members begin to argue sharply about blame, the chair should **pause, restate the item and steer the discussion back to solutions**. Remind members to speak to the issue, not the person. If it continues, call a short break.

An important new issue that needs research should be **noted and placed on a later agenda**, with papers. This protects members who are not present and gives time for facts. Only a real emergency should be decided at once.

ul: A **conflict of interest** exists when a member could gain or lose personally from a decision (a relative bidding for a contract, for example). The member should **declare it, and stay out of the discussion and decision** as the rules say. The minutes record the declaration.
**Confidential items**, such as a disciplinary case, must be marked confidential and shared only with those entitled to see them. Spare paper copies should be collected and shredded.
Members must not repeat confidential matters outside the meeting.

blocks.p: A good close **sums up decisions and actions, repeats who does what and by when, and confirms the date of the next meeting**. Thank members. End on time.

Minutes are the official record of a meeting. They record **decisions, actions, owners and dates**, not every word. They protect the organisation if a decision is questioned, and tell absent members what was agreed.

head: Type
What it records
Used for
rows: Action minutes
Decisions and actions only, in a short form
Most staff and project meetings
Summary minutes
Decisions, plus a brief outline of the main points of discussion
Committees and boards
Verbatim record
Every word spoken
Rare: legal or inquiry hearings

ul: Name of the meeting, date, time and place (or platform).
Who attended, and who sent apologies. Note the time of arrival or departure if it affects the quorum.
Declarations of interest and how they were handled.
For each item: the decision, the action, the **person responsible** and the **deadline**.
Numbers of votes for a vote, if the rules require.
The time the meeting closed and the date of the next one.
Signature of the chair and date of approval.
Plain, neutral, in the past tense and the third person.
Record what was agreed, not who said what (unless a member asks that a view be recorded).
No personal opinions, comments about people or gossip.
Be accurate with figures and dates.

head: Poor
Better
rows: Mr Brown said the delay was the fault of the lazy dispatch team.
The meeting noted that deliveries were delayed by two days.
It was decided that something would be done about the stock.
The meeting agreed that Ms Reid would count the stock by 20 November.
We argued about the purchase for ages.
The meeting agreed to delay the purchase until March.

blocks.note: Good minutes are written for the person who was not there. Could they read your minutes and know exactly what to do?
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: An **action log** is a table of tasks, owners and due dates, usually kept in a spreadsheet and carried from meeting to meeting.

head: No.
Action
Owner
Due date
Status
rows: Get three quotations for the generator
Mr Edwards
15 December
Open
Send revised leave form to all staff
Ms Francis
30 November
Done
Report cost of overtime in October
Ms Clarke
7 December
Open

blocks.p: Every action has **one owner** and a **due date**. 'All staff' as an owner usually means nobody does it.

flow: Secretary drafts minutes within a few working days
Chair checks the draft
Draft sent to members, marked DRAFT
Next meeting: members check accuracy; errors corrected
Minutes approved and signed
Approved minutes and action points sent to members and action owners; filed

blocks.p: If a member says a decision is recorded wrongly, the meeting **agrees a correction** and then approves the minutes as corrected. Approved minutes are not changed afterwards without a formal decision.

head: When
What to do
rows: Before
Invite only those entitled; mark papers 'Confidential'; send them securely (password or hand delivery); keep personal details out of the notice and agenda
During
Remind members of confidentiality; check no one unauthorised is in the room or on the call; take a confidential item in a separate part of the meeting if some members must leave
After
Collect or shred spare copies; keep confidential minutes in a locked cabinet or password file; share only with those entitled; dispose of them as the policy says

ul: Keep approved minutes in a secure, organised file, on paper or electronically, as the organisation's **records policy** says.
Under the data protection law, collect and keep only the personal information you need. Do not put a staff member's health or private details in minutes if the record does not need them.
Limit access to confidential minutes; use passwords for electronic files.
Dispose of records as the policy and the law require.

sections.title: Following up and evaluating the meeting

blocks.p: A meeting has not worked until the actions are done. After the meeting:

flow: Send approved minutes and action points to members and owners
Update the action log
Remind owners before each due date
Check progress at the next meeting under matters arising
Escalate actions that are stuck

blocks.p: If actions are overdue, the meeting manager should **first contact each owner to find out progress and any barriers** (resources, unclear tasks, competing work), then help to remove them. Blame comes last.
The best evidence that a meeting was effective is that **its outcomes were reached and acted on**. Other signs:

head: Measure
How to find out
rows: Outcome reached
Did the meeting decide what it set out to decide?
Actions completed on time
Actions done on time ÷ total actions × 100. For example 9 of 12 on time = 75%
Started and finished on time
Check the clock against the agenda
Cost against value
Staff-time cost compared with the result
Participation
Did everyone who needed to speak do so?
Member feedback
A short survey after the meeting

blocks.p: A **short anonymous survey** (three or four questions: was the purpose clear, was time well used, did I get a chance to speak, what one change would help) gives honest answers. Review results, tell members what you will change, and change it.

blocks.h: A three-month plan to improve a firm's meetings

head: Month
Action
rows: List all regular meetings, who attends, how long they last and what they cost; survey staff; set a purpose for each
Cut or merge meetings with no purpose; introduce timed agendas, papers in advance and action logs; train chairs and secretaries
Repeat the survey; compare cost, time and action completion with month 1; report the results and agree the next steps

ul: Shorten or drop meetings that no longer have a purpose.
Invite fewer people, or invite people for part of the agenda only.
Send papers earlier.
Use a standing agenda with timed items.
Train members and secretaries in minute-taking and chairing.
decide whether a meeting is needed and write its purpose and outcome.
choose the right type of meeting and the right people to invite.
plan date, time, venue or platform, access needs and notice that meet the organisation's rules.
build a timed agenda with decisions early, and send papers with the notice.
work out the staff-time cost of a meeting.
prepare and run an online or hybrid meeting that includes everyone.
chair a meeting: check the quorum, keep to time, manage talkative and quiet members, and handle conflict.
explain motions, seconders, amendments, voting and casting votes.
apply rules on conflicts of interest and confidentiality.
write clear, neutral minutes with decisions, actions, owners and dates, and an action log.
handle draft and approved minutes, corrections and records under the data protection law.
follow up actions and judge whether a meeting was effective.

terms: The list of items to be dealt with at a meeting, in order, often with times.
The smallest number of members who must be present for decisions to be valid.
The official record of a meeting: decisions, actions, owners and dates.
A table of actions with owners, due dates and status.
Names of members who told the secretary they could not attend.
Follow-up on points from the last minutes.
The written rules for running meetings.
A formal proposal put to a meeting.
The chair's extra vote used to break a tie, if the rules allow.
Agreement everyone can accept after discussion.
A meeting with some members in the room and some online.
A situation where a member's personal interest could affect a decision.
To stop a meeting and continue it later.
The member who supports a motion so that it can be debated.
A meeting in which every member joins from a different place online.
People multiplied by hours, a measure of staff time used.
The message giving members the date, time and place of a meeting.

c1.title: A school board decides on a roof repair
c1.text: The board of a primary school in May Pen, Clarendon, has nine members. Its standing orders say the quorum is five, notice is seven days and decisions are made by majority vote. The agenda has apologies, declarations of interest, the last minutes, matters arising, a decision on repairing the staff-room roof, the principal's report and any other business. Three quotations for the roof, between J$1,450,000 and J$1,900,000, were handed to members at the start of the meeting. Five members were present at the start; one leaves after an hour, before the roof vote.

c2.title: The Monday sales meeting at a furniture store
c2.text: Tanesha Williams manages a furniture store in Portmore with 12 staff. Every Monday she holds a meeting of all 12 at 8 a.m. that often runs 90 minutes. Each person costs the business about J$2,000 an hour. Much of the time goes on stock news that concerns only the warehouse team, and no one is sure what the meeting is meant to achieve. The store opens at 9:30 a.m.

c3.title: A hybrid project meeting for a construction firm
c3.text: A construction firm based in Kingston holds a weekly project meeting. Three managers sit in the Kingston boardroom, a quantity surveyor joins online from Montego Bay, and the site engineer joins from a building site near Ocho Rios where the signal is weak. Last week the online members heard little of the room discussion, the site engineer dropped out twice, and a stranger joined after the link was posted in a public group chat.

c4.title: A credit union loan committee
c4.text: The credit committee of a credit union in St Ann has seven members. Its rules set the quorum at four. At tonight's meeting the committee will decide a loan application from the sister of member Everton Anderson. The loan papers contain the applicant's income details. Everton has said at the start that he has an interest in this item.

c5.title: Minutes from a clinic administration meeting
c5.text: Mrs Hyacinth Campbell chairs the monthly meeting of the administration office of a health centre in Savanna-la-Mar. The secretary's draft minutes contain the line 'Nurse Gray said the front desk staff are lazy', a patient's full name and address, and the action 'Check the clinic appointment rota - all staff'. Over the last three meetings, 12 actions were agreed and 9 were done on time.

questions.q: Before the roof vote, the member leaves and four members remain. What should the chair do?
o: Let the four remaining members vote, as the item was debated while five were present
Ask the member who left to confirm her vote by phone from the corridor
Note that the quorum is lost and defer the vote to a meeting that has a quorum
Take the vote and ask the five members to approve it at the next meeting
questions.why: Decisions need a quorum at the time they are taken. With four of a required five, the meeting can talk but cannot make a valid decision, so the vote must wait.

questions.q: At which point in the agenda should the chair ask members to declare any personal interest in the roof contract?
o: Early, after apologies and before the items on which an interest could arise
Just before the vote, once the discussion of the quotations is over
At the end of the meeting, under any other business, so it does not slow the items
Only if a member objects to another member's part in the discussion of the item
questions.why: Declarations come near the start so that a member with an interest can be kept out of the discussion as well as the vote, and so that the record is complete.

questions.q: The three quotations were first seen at the start of the meeting. What is the best action for the chair on this J$1,450,000 to J$1,900,000 decision?
o: Ask the treasurer to read all three quotations aloud, then take the vote straight away
Choose the lowest quotation at once, since the principal says the roof is leaking
Vote on the highest quotation, since it should give the longest-lasting roof
Defer the decision and send the quotations with the next notice
questions.why: Papers for a decision should reach members in time to read them. A large spending decision made on papers seen for the first time is hard to defend. A short delay is cheaper than a poor decision.

questions.q: A member says, 'I move that we accept the lowest quotation.' What is normally needed before the board can debate this motion?
o: The principal must agree to it
Another member must second it
The treasurer must confirm the money
The chair must vote for it first
questions.why: In formal meetings a motion is debated only when a second member supports it. This shows that more than one person wants it discussed.

questions.q: Tanesha's meeting has 12 people and runs 90 minutes. At J$2,000 an hour each, what is the staff-time cost of one meeting?
questions.why: 12 people × J$2,000 × 1.5 hours = J$36,000. Over a 50-week year this is J$1,800,000.

questions.q: Which first change would do most to stop the Monday meeting drifting?
o: Move the meeting to a different day of the week so that more staff can attend
Ask every member to bring a written report to every Monday meeting
Add a second meeting on Fridays so that nothing is missed during the week
Give each meeting a stated purpose and a timed agenda, and close it when done
questions.why: A meeting with no purpose fills the time given to it. A stated outcome and timed items let the chair keep to the point and end on time.

questions.q: The warehouse team is the only group affected by most stock news. How should Tanesha handle this?
o: Take stock news in a short warehouse meeting and release the others
Keep all staff in the room, since the others might learn something useful from it
Let the others leave the meeting quietly whenever the warehouse items start
Drop stock news from all meetings and mention it on the notice board instead
questions.why: People should be invited for the items that concern them. A separate short briefing saves the time of staff who do not need the news and still gets the news to those who do.

questions.q: The store opens at 9:30 a.m. and the full meeting starts at 8 a.m. After Tanesha shortens it, what should she arrange to make sure the shop is still served?
o: Open the store late whenever a meeting happens to run over time
Ask customers to wait at the door until the meeting has ended
Finish before opening time, or rotate cover for the shop floor
Hold the meeting in the busiest hour so that nobody forgets to attend it
questions.why: Planning a meeting includes arranging cover so customers are still served. Timing it before opening, or rotating cover, protects both service and sales.

questions.q: Which set-up best helps the Montego Bay surveyor follow the Kingston boardroom discussion?
o: A laptop at one end of the table, with everyone speaking as they normally do
A phone in the middle of the table, with the chair repeating each remark aloud
A room microphone and speaker, a table camera and one speaker at a time
Written notes of the discussion sent to the surveyor after the meeting has ended
questions.why: Equipment that picks up the whole room, plus an agreement to speak one at a time, lets online members hear and take part during the meeting rather than afterwards.

questions.q: The site engineer's signal is weak. Which arrangement is the most useful back-up?
o: A telephone dial-in number, and a written update sent before the meeting
A promise from the site engineer to move to a better signal during the meeting
Cancelling the engineer's item and recording it in the minutes as noted
Asking the engineer to join from a nearby cafe the same afternoon
questions.why: Planning for a known weak point gives certainty. A phone line works on a poor signal and a written update means the engineer's information is not lost if the call drops.

questions.q: A stranger joined after the link was posted in a public group chat. What should the organiser do next time?
o: Ask members to type their names in the chat as they join each week
Tell members not to discuss sensitive items while online with the group
Start the meeting before the link is sent out to anyone outside the firm
Send the link only to invited members, with a waiting room or password
questions.why: Controlling who can join protects confidential items. A private link with a waiting room or password stops people who were not invited from entering.

questions.q: Online members keep waiting for a chance to speak. What should the chair do?
o: Ask online members to put their questions in writing after the meeting is over
Invite online members to speak first on each item and check before moving on
Ask online members to speak up loudly and interrupt when they need to
Let online members choose which items they want to speak on during the meeting
questions.why: In a hybrid meeting it is easy for those online to be overlooked. The chair must give them a regular, planned chance to speak.

questions.q: Everton has declared his interest. What should the secretary record in the minutes?
o: Only that Everton was present for the whole of the meeting as a member
The declaration, and that he took no part in the discussion or decision
The declaration, but not what he did during the discussion of the item
Nothing, since the interest is a private matter for Everton to deal with
questions.why: The minutes should show that the interest was declared and that the member stood aside. This protects both the member and the committee if the loan is questioned later.

questions.q: The loan papers hold the applicant's income details. What should happen to spare paper copies?
o: Leave them on the table for the cleaner to throw out with the rubbish
Let members take them home so that they can read them again
Photograph them and share the photos in the members' group chat
Collect and shred them at the end, or return them to the secretary
questions.why: Confidential papers should reach only those entitled to see them, and unneeded copies should be destroyed securely. This protects the applicant's privacy.

questions.q: Everton leaves the room for the loan item. Can the committee still decide?
o: Yes, because six members remain and the quorum is four
No, because the committee now has fewer than seven members
Yes, but only if Everton agrees to vote by message
No, because the application can only be decided by the full committee
questions.why: Quorum is the number the rules require, not the full membership. Six members remain and four are enough, so the committee can validly decide.

questions.q: The committee votes on the loan. What should the minutes record about the vote?
o: Only the names of those members who voted against the motion
Everything each member said in the discussion before the voting began
The motion, the result, and the numbers for, against and abstaining
That the decision was unanimous, whatever the actual count of the votes
questions.why: Minutes record the decision and the result accurately. Recording the numbers, where required, makes the decision traceable without writing down every word.

questions.q: Which rewrite makes the action 'Check the clinic appointment rota - all staff' a proper action?
o: Check the appointment rota carefully and quickly as soon as time allows: front desk team
All front desk staff to share the rota check as part of their normal work
Check the rota for December clashes: Ms S. Lewis, by 20 November
The appointment rota should be checked by someone before the next meeting
questions.why: A useful action has one named owner, a clear task and a due date. 'All staff' or 'someone' usually means nobody does it.

questions.q: What should the secretary do with the line 'Nurse Gray said the front desk staff are lazy'?
o: Leave out the personal comment and record the decision reached
Keep it so that the minutes are a complete record of what was said
Keep it, and add the name of the person who disagreed with it
Move it to the end of the minutes under any other business
questions.why: Minutes are neutral and record decisions, actions and key points, not personal remarks. A comment about colleagues can cause harm and adds nothing to what was agreed.

questions.q: Nine of the twelve actions were done on time. What is the on-time completion rate?
questions.why: 9 ÷ 12 × 100 = 75%. The rate shows whether the meeting is turning decisions into results.

questions.q: The draft minutes are sent to members before the next meeting. How should they be marked?
o: As APPROVED, so that members can act on them
As DRAFT, not yet approved
As CONFIDENTIAL, because no meeting has seen them
As FINAL, once the chair has read them
questions.why: Minutes are not the official record until the next meeting has checked them for accuracy and approved them. Marking them as a draft makes this clear.
